What is matter?

Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space (that is, has volume). Almost everything around you is matter: your exercise book, the water in your bottle, the air you breathe, the sand in the compound, your own body. Matter is made up of extremely tiny particles — atoms and molecules — that are far too small to see. Even air, which you cannot see, is matter: it has mass and takes up space, which you can prove by blowing up a balloon and watching it expand and become slightly heavier. Things that are NOT matter include light, heat, sound and electricity — these are forms of energy, because they have no mass and occupy no space. Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid and gas.

What are the three states of matter and how do they differ?

Matter exists in three states, differing in how their particles are arranged. SOLIDS have particles packed tightly in a fixed pattern, vibrating in place; so a solid has a definite shape and a definite volume — a stone, a table, a block of ice. LIQUIDS have particles close together but able to slide over one another; so a liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container — water, kerosene, palm oil. GASES have particles far apart and moving freely at high speed; so a gas has neither definite shape nor definite volume and fills any container completely — air, cooking gas, steam. Compressibility follows the spacing: gases squash easily (which is why cooking gas fits in a cylinder), liquids barely, and solids almost not at all.

What are the changes of state of matter?

Matter changes state when heat is added or removed.

MELTING: solid to liquid, as ice becomes water in a warm room. FREEZING (solidification): liquid to solid, as water becomes ice in the freezer.
EVAPORATION or BOILING: liquid to gas, as water becomes steam over a fire.
CONDENSATION: gas to liquid, as steam becomes droplets on a cold plate.
SUBLIMATION: solid straight to gas without passing through liquid, as with camphor (the balls used to keep clothes fresh) and dry ice.
DEPOSITION: gas straight back to solid.

Notice the pattern: adding heat pushes matter towards gas because particles gain energy and spread apart; removing heat pushes it towards solid. Importantly, these are PHYSICAL changes — no new substance forms, and they can be reversed.

What is the difference between a physical change and a chemical change?

A PHYSICAL change alters only the appearance or state of a substance — no new substance is formed, and the change can usually be reversed. Examples: melting ice, boiling water, dissolving sugar in water, breaking a stick, grinding pepper. The sugar is still sugar; evaporate the water and you get it back. A CHEMICAL change produces one or more NEW substances with different properties, and it is usually irreversible, often accompanied by heat, light, gas bubbles, or a colour change. Examples: burning firewood (you cannot turn ash back into wood), cooking an egg, milk turning sour, iron rusting, and food digesting in your stomach. Quick test: ask yourself, 'Is it still the same substance?' If yes, it is physical; if a new substance has appeared, it is chemical.

Prove to me that air is matter

Air is invisible, so let us prove it has mass and occupies space with simple experiments. EXPERIMENT 1 (air occupies space): push an empty inverted cup straight down into a bucket of water. The water does not fill the cup, because the trapped air is already occupying that space. Tilt the cup slightly and you will see air bubbles escape as water rushes in to take its place. EXPERIMENT 2 (air has mass): balance a metre rule with an identical deflated balloon tied at each end. Now inflate one balloon and re-hang it — that side dips down, showing the air added mass. EXPERIMENT 3 (air resists): blow up a balloon and feel it push back as it stretches. Since air has both mass and volume, it satisfies the definition of matter perfectly.

What is the particulate nature of matter?

The particulate nature of matter means that all matter is made up of tiny particles that are constantly in motion, with spaces between them. Three everyday observations prove it.

First, DIFFUSION: when your mother is frying stew in the kitchen, you smell it from the sitting room, because odour particles move and spread through the air.
Second, DISSOLVING: stir sugar into water and it disappears, because the sugar particles fit into the spaces between the water particles — notice the water level barely rises.
Third, COMPRESSION: you can squeeze a lot of gas into a small cooking-gas cylinder because gas particles have large spaces between them. Particles move fastest in gases, slower in liquids and merely vibrate in solids, and heating always makes them move faster.

Why does a bottle of water burst when you put it in the freezer?

This happens because water is unusual — it EXPANDS when it freezes, unlike most substances which contract. In liquid water the particles are close together and move around freely. As the temperature drops below 0°C, the particles lock into a fixed open framework of ice crystals with larger spaces between them. That structure takes up about 9% more volume than the same water did as a liquid. Inside a sealed bottle filled to the brim, the growing ice has nowhere to go, so it pushes hard on the walls until the plastic splits or the cap pops. This is also why ice floats on water (it is less dense), why pipes burst in cold countries, and why you should never fill a bottle completely before freezing it — always leave space at the top.

How can I separate a mixture of sand and salt?

You can separate them using the fact that salt dissolves in water but sand does not.

Step 1: DISSOLVING — pour the mixture into water and stir well. The salt dissolves to form a solution, while the sand stays as solid grains.
Step 2: FILTRATION — pour the mixture through filter paper (a clean cloth works too). The sand is trapped as residue on the filter, while the salt solution passes through as filtrate.
Step 3: EVAPORATION — heat the salt solution gently in an evaporating dish. The water evaporates as vapour, leaving dry salt crystals behind. Now you have both substances separated and pure. This same three-step principle is used to obtain salt from seawater in coastal areas, and it is a favourite BECE practical question — learn the three terms: residue, filtrate, evaporation.
